stories.headline: Update: US-Iran War Continues With No Clear Exit Strategy as Talks Resume
stories.summary:
The United States and Iran remain locked in an active military conflict, with renewed strikes this week and no clear path to resolution for either side. Trump stated in a Time magazine interview that the U.S. could escalate strikes on Iran after November's midterm elections, while Iran's foreign minister said Tehran is awaiting the "definitive views" of mediators before committing to a position. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian delivered a defiant speech to the UN after Trump threatened to "annihilate" Iran if a peace deal is not reached.

The conflict is having broad economic consequences, with diesel prices in the United Kingdom reaching an all-time high of 200.01 pence per litre. A USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group has been deployed for one of the longest naval deployments in recent memory, and the Pentagon evacuated American bombers from British bases in a move analysts described as reflecting concern about escalation. An oil tanker in the region sustained damage from projectile strikes, with casualties reported.

Diplomatically, the two sides held their first direct talks since a ceasefire collapsed in June, with exchanges of fire continuing intermittently. The death of Supreme Leader Khamenei has reshuffled Iran's leadership, adding uncertainty about Tehran's strategic intentions. Analysts say none of the options available to Iran's new leaders offers a clear path to victory.

The conflict has drawn in allied nations, with the UK's HMS Dragon deployed to the eastern Mediterranean. Supporters of continued U.S. military pressure argue Iran's nuclear ambitions justify the campaign; critics, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, called Trump's rhetoric about annihilating Iran "deranged." The White House defended the president's language as a warning about nuclear risk.

stories.headline: Update: UAE Says Flydubai Co-Pilot's Radicalization Began During Australian Studies
stories.summary:
UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said Friday that Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, who allegedly attempted to crash a Flydubai flight into Tel Aviv's airport on September 30, first showed signs of radicalization in 2017 while studying in Australia. Al-Shamsi said interrogations revealed the pilot was inspired by al-Qaeda's September 11 attacks and had "intensified his exposure to material promoting terrorism" in the period leading up to the attack. The pilot wounded the captain with an emergency crash axe before being overpowered by passengers; an Indian co-pilot managed to land the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia with more than 170 people on board.

The UAE's state news agency reported that al-Hammami trained physically in boxing and prepared psychologically for the suicide attack, acting alone according to his own account, though investigators said they were continuing to verify that claim. Australian authorities confirmed the man held a student visa from 2014 and studied in the country between 2015 and 2017. Tweets from his since-deleted account described those years abroad as "the golden years of my religious commitment."

Australia's Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team, comprising federal police, state police, and the ASIO security agency, confirmed it is investigating his Australian connections. Questions have been raised about security vetting procedures at Flydubai and how the attacker received clearance to fly a plane carrying Israeli-bound passengers. The incident has prompted calls for tighter screening of airline crew.

stories.headline: Three Convicted of Murdering Australian Brothers and U.S. Friend in Mexico Surfing Trip
stories.summary:
A Mexican court found three men guilty Friday of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their American friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip to Baja California in 2024. The defendants, identified only as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco, and Ángel Jesús for legal reasons, killed the tourists in an apparent botched robbery in a secluded beach area; the victims' bodies were later found in a well with gunshot wounds to their heads. Sentencing has not yet occurred, but prosecution sought 150 years in prison for each defendant.

The brothers' parents, Debra and Martin Robinson, attended the month-long trial in Ensenada and delivered emotional testimony. "It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," Martin Robinson told the court. Family members of Carter Rhoad joined the proceedings by video link from the United States.

The murders in 2024 drew international attention because Ensenada is generally considered a safer destination for surfers relative to other parts of Mexico. The killings prompted local surfers and residents to call for improved security in the state, where tourism is a major economic driver. A girlfriend of the alleged ringleader was separately convicted in 2025 and sentenced to 20 years.

stories.headline: UK to Try First Person Charged Over 1994 Rwanda Genocide in October 2027
stories.summary:
A British judge set a provisional trial date of October 2027 for Dr. Vincent Brown, formerly known as Dr. Vincent Bajinya, making him the first person in the United Kingdom to face charges related to the 1994 Rwandan genocide. The 65-year-old London resident appeared via video link from Belmarsh prison Friday for a pre-trial hearing at the Old Bailey, where Justice Cheema-Grubb scheduled an eight-to-twelve-week trial. Brown is charged with one count of conduct ancillary to genocide and six counts of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity; he has indicated he will plead not guilty.

Prosecutors allege Brown was a party to six murders between April 6 and 13, 1994, during the height of the genocide, in which an estimated 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu Rwandans were killed over 100 days. Brown had served as head of Rwanda's Department of Family Health before the genocide. A British investigation lasting seven years led to the charges.

The case is significant as a test of the United Kingdom's capacity and willingness to prosecute genocide suspects living within its borders under international humanitarian law. A plea and case management hearing was set for January 15. The court noted that a £100,000 bail condition imposed earlier in October had not yet been met, keeping Brown in custody.
